Major(s) News & Notes, April 30th, 2026
McIlroy emerges. PGA's 20 are set. Rose's shock move before return to Philly. Sunningdale to host Women's Open. WGHOF accepts public noms. Jack v. Tiger Q&A w/Harig. Quotables. This. That. Reads.
Days to the PGA Championship first round: 14
Forecast:
70s/low 80s w/possible late t-storms on the weekendDays to the U.S. Women’s Open first round: 36

Rory McIlroy resurfaced at Tuesday night’s state dinner after (hopefully) enjoying the quietest post-Masters victory celebration in modern memory. He even got an impromptu callout to commemorate his second straight win.
But when you couple his zenful post-win existence with that matter-of-fact, just-another-step-in-the-journey post-win press conference, it’s easy to start wondering: might McIlroy be leaning toward an old school, old man schedule over the next few years? One that combines notes of post-accident Hogan with early Nicklaus-still-making-his-own-yardage-books-ahead-of-a-major? A schedule where McIlroy makes his four major appearances, throws in a few favorites at great layouts, and fills out his season playing national Opens (encouraged by generous appearance fees and the good vibes coming with actually growing the game globally).
The 2026 Masters champion is committed to next week’s Truist Championship before heading on to Aronimink in search of a third Wannamaker Trophy and seventh major. But in winning after taking several weeks off with a B- game that fed off of his deep dive into a crispier-than-normal Augusta National, McIlroy exuded a quiet confidence even after only winning by a stroke. His demeanor exuded a contentment realized from beating the best in the game using immense skill and combining it with a local knowledge-fueled short game performance to make up for an unexpectedly balky driver.
It’s not yet clear whether he’s been destroying his carbon footprint to fly up and study Aronimink in a similar fashion. Or if he’s changed his mind about his major championship approach since putting the Green Jacket (back) on.
“I’m not going to take three weeks off before every major, but to get to the major venues early, do your preparation, play, and not just play and look at things, but actually play,” he said on Sunday of the Masters. “Go out there with one ball, shoot a score, and try to do it that way.”
So why is he bothering with Quail Hollow when he could spend time batting it around a nuanced Donald Ross course (where he finished 5th/-18 in 2018)?
If McIlroy had qualms about saying no to old buddy Johnny Harris, his Truist feelings of affection may diminish quickly next week when he gets his 23rd question about welcoming back LIV defectors.
The demise of Saudi Arabia’s stolen pet project appears to be uber-imminent.
Various Friedballs and Baffling Cleeks and Roman Lesions are reportedly dialing up the Global Home in hopes of joining the Returning Members Program.
The LIV unraveling morass is all quite entertaining unless you’re a lover of golf history who heard McIlroy’s tone and saw the look in his eyes Sunday night of the Masters. He wants to win a bunch more majors, pronto. He’s surveyed the current landscape and, other than Scottie Scheffler, there’s zero reason to rule out trying for the Grand Slam this year.
So please, Golf Gods, don’t let this LIV mess deprive us any more than it already has. Pretty please?
Meanwhile, in on-course news, The Quad is way past its Substack bandwidth limit this week. But there’s a lot to get to! Starting with the PGA of America, determining the 20 professionals headed to Aronimink following four rounds at Bandon Dunes. Then we’ll get to a ton of (mostly) good news and notes befitting the heart of the major season, including a big return of Sunningdale to the major calendar.
The PGA’s 20
A lively four days at Bandon Dunes saw the game’s very best at folding a quarter zips (cashmere, too!) finish their battle for the right to play at Aronimink this year.
Jesse Droemer of Riverbend in Houston, Texas, emerged with Walter Hagen Cup to win the 2026 PGA Professional Championship. Droemer posted an impressive four-under-par total in occasional gale-force(ish) winds.
“I knew the conditions were going to be tough,” said Droemer, the fifth champion from the Southern Texas PGA Section. “I really was trying to embrace the elements. I’m glad it was windy.”
Besides Droemer, others who will make the journey as part of the “Corebridge Financial 20” by qualifying for the second major of the year:
Ben Kern (GM at Hickory Hills in South Bloomfield, Ohio) finished second at 3-under after shooting a final-round 1-under-par 71.
Michael Kartrude (Royal Palm Beach, Fla.) took third at 2-under after posting 2-under-par 70.
Defending Champion Tyler Collet (assistant at John’s Island in Vero Beach, Fla.), Zach Haynes (The Club at Olde Stone, Bowling Green, Ky.), Garrett Sapp (San Gabriel CC, San Marino, Calif.) and Austin Hurt (head pro at Wing Point on Bainbridge Island, Wash.) tied for fourth at 1-under.
And Blockie made it after a T10.
Past Champions Ben Polland (Wilson, Wyo.) and Michael Block (Mission Viejo, Calif.) were two of the eight players T-10 at 1-over-par 288.
Chris Gabriele (Halesite, N.Y.), also T-10, eagled the par-5 18th hole to make it safely.
Braden Shattuck (T8) of the Philadelphia section’s Rolling Green Golf Club qualified for his third PGA. He will be the closest competitor to hold a home region advantage.
Sabrina Bonanno (Redmond, Wash.) led the nine women in the field, shooting even-par 72 to finish T-34 at 5-over-par 292.
The 20 headed to Aronimink:
Rose Makes Team Papaya Move Ahead Of Philly Return!?
Justin Rose captured his first and only major in the suburbs of Philadelphia.
He won a tour event at pre-restoration Aronimink and lost in a 2018 playoff to Keegan Bradley on the post-restoration version. While just a 35-1 shot in the betting world, it’s not a stretch to label Rose the PGA favorite after the 45-year-old once again contended at the Masters.
But after making a mid-season equipment switch?
The same player whose infamous one-year early exit deal with Honma? While rumored for a while, it’s still a head-scratcher to see Rose dumping his Miura irons mid-season while leading the Tour in greens hit (72%) and ranking seventh in Strokes Gained Approach.
He will replace them with new McLaren Golf blades this week at Doral. Judging by the look of the irons from Greg Moore’s on-site GolfWRX images, the new clubs haven’t seen much action.
Rose is the Formula 1 brand’s first golf ambassador and will carry their signature papaya-shaded bag as an investor in the startup that’s pricing the clubs at $375. Each. Or just $2,625 for a 4-PW set with no discount for being stupid enough buying a full set.
“I'm looking to mitigate risk,” Rose said of the switch. “Yeah, I've done this once before as well in 2019 obviously and I kind of learned a lot from that process. So I feel a bit better place now to kind of go down this path. I think yeah, I think there's some best practices that we're kind of, we've sort of put into development really that I think are giving me what I feel are a fantastic set of golf clubs.”
The notoriously meticulous Rose says range data shows the new clubs “outperforming” what he’s been using.
“That's the exciting part for me,” he said in Miami. “Obviously there's going to be a refinement process. You can test all you want, you got to get the clubs in play, and there's going to be little mini situations out there, different lies, all sorts of things, just getting comfortable. But in the long-term, no, I don't see there being an issue at all.
There is the possibility that a wiser and often beyond-meticulous Rose has extensively tested the clubs to ensure there will be no disruptions. And it’s not like he’s putting something in his bag as hellacious-looking as the Honma driver that he won with before souring on the clubs enough to get out of a long-term deal. But it’s still an audacious move ahead of a major that’s set up for Rose to conquer.
Sunningdale To Host 2028 AIG Women’s Open
For the first time in two decades, the world’s leading women’s golfers will return to Sunningdale’s Old Course.
The 2028 AIG Women’s Open will be played at Sunningdale from August 14-20th, two weeks after the conclusion of the women’s golf competition in the Olympic Games.
Sunningdale was most recently seen during the 2024 Curtis Cup and, before that, the 2021 Rolex Senior Open.
The Willie Park Jr.-designed Old dates to 1901 and was modified by club secretary H.S. Colt, designer of the New Course.
Previous Open winners at Sunningdale include Karrie Webb (1997), Se Ri Pak (2001), Karen Stupples (2004), and Jiyai Shin (2008). Webb’s record-setting 269 in 1997 was matched by Stupples in 2004, who posted the lowest final round by a Women’s Open champion with a 64.
"Our Club is firmly committed to supporting the continued growth and increasing significance of the AIG Women’s Open within the global game,” said Paul Chase-Gardener, Chairman of Sunningdale. “We look forward to welcoming the world’s leading players, officials and spectators to Sunningdale and to presenting the Old Course as a true and memorable test of golf as befitting this Championship.”
Purse And Coverage Expansion For The AIG Women’s Open
This year’s 50th playing of the AIG Women’s Open will see a prize fund bump to $10 million and additional three hours per day of live coverage.
The prize fund for the inaugural Women’s Open won by Jenny Lee Smith?
£500.
For rounds one and two at Royal Lytham & St Annes this year, the R&A announced that an early window from 9 am to 1 pm BST will feature the morning marquee groups. Full main coverage will continue from 1 pm to 7 pm BST on Thursday and Friday, and from 12 pm to 7 pm BST on Saturday and Sunday. It’s not clear how much the R&A’s unpredictable, multi-split-up-but-not-really American media partners will carry the action.
This year’s championship will be played at Lytham from July 29th to August 2nd.
Pricey Ireland-Only Ryder Cup Tix Sell Out
The “exclusive priority window” for residents of Ireland sold out in under four hours, according to Ryder Cup Europe. Exact sales of the €499 ticket were not revealed, but “more than 150,000 people from across the island of Ireland had pre-registered for early access.”
A second general admission sale for fans worldwide opens on Wednesday, June 3.
The €499 price point was labeled a “sad day” for loyal supporters by Ryder Cup great Ian Poulter, while website issues rankled already peeved fans.
According to Gambling.com’s analysis of the prices, the 2027 matches have risen 640% since 2010 at Celtic Manor.
Quotable
Scottie Scheffler on playing the week before majors. “Major championships are just the hardest events. When you look at the courses we're playing for our Signature Events now, like, I mean, I think it was a couple years ago we did Jack's place and the US Open back-to-back. I'm like, I physically and mentally, I can't do this for two weeks in a row. I won Memorial and I was whipped showing up to the US Open. So that's kind of how I adjusted my schedule to be like, oh, you know, maybe the week before the major it's not wise to go out there and beat myself up a little bit. Maybe it's best for me to stay home and get ready for the tournament. Just because you look at the demands of a regular week, a major championship is times 10.”
Justin Rose on 2028 Open host Royal Lytham & St Annes. “More of like an inland feeling links than a very coastal. You feel like you're in a little town. There's some trees around. You feel a little cocooned at times. Good golf course though. Technically a good golf course. But, with respect, not one of the most beautiful, or not one that's on my radar of like my favorites. But as a technical test of golf, like really, really good.”
Adam Scott on nearing 100 straight majors. “I don't know what to make of it. I mean, part of me doesn't want to be the guy yet who just has all these other things that aren't based around winning events. I would rather win some stuff, and let's celebrate winning the US Open than just playing in it.”
Keegan Bradley on Jim Furyk’s appointment to succeed him as Ryder Cup captain.“I think that’s a point you wouldn’t hear from the players; I think the players are excited. I think the best thing to do is to have a known commodity, a sort of reset here.”
WGHOF Accepting Nominations
The World Golf Hall of Fame has opened up nominations for the Class of 2027, the first time in the WGHOF’s history that members of the public are invited to submit nominations.
“We are thrilled to kick off the selection process for the 2027 induction ceremony in St Andrews,” said Mike Trostel, director of the World Golf Hall of Fame. “By making nominations open to the public, we believe golf fans will be more invested in the process and it will ensure that all worthy candidates are considered for the Class of 2027.”
The nomination period runs through July 31, 2026, and nominations will be accepted in four categories:
Male Competitor: Must be age 45 or older, or retired from competition for three or more years at the time of the ceremony. First-time eligible players include Justin Rose, Adam Scott and Sergio Garcia.
Female Competitor: Must be age 45 or older, or retired from competition for three or more years at the time of the ceremony. First-time eligible players include Suzann Pettersen.
Contributor: Individuals who have made their biggest impact on the game outside of the competitive arena. This group includes architects, teachers, media members, golf administrators, instructors and innovators.
Historic Player/Amateur: Competitors who accomplished the majority of their wins either more than 50 years ago from the year of the upcoming induction ceremony (pre-1977) or as amateurs.
You can submit nominations here.
Q&A With Bob Harig: Tiger v. Jack
The longtime golf writer’s latest book opens with the unexpected way the two met at Bel Air Country Club in Los Angeles, before going on to compare the careers of Jack Nicklaus and Tiger Woods in an entertaining and breezy read.
Quad: Why take on the task of match-playing Jack v. Tiger?
BH: The subtitle of the book is Golf’s Great Debate and I don’t think that is far off. It’s been a topic discussed for years, well before Tiger even got halfway to Jack’s major total. Who is the greatest champion? Who is the greatest player? It just seemed a logical time to examine the argument. The 40th anniversary of Jack’s last win at the 1986 Masters and Tiger just turned 50, so comparing and contrasting them to that point in their lives and careers leads to a lot of discussion and, of course, how we got here, how the majors evolved, why they are important, and others who might factor in are also part of the story.
Quad: Who was the most engaging interview?
BH: There were several who were very good. Jack was very good in a lengthy session at his Florida office. His memory of details from his 1962 rookie season, for example, is quite impressive. Brandel Chamblee provided excellent insight, as did broadcaster David Feherty. Hank Haney, who coached Woods from 2004 to 2010, was quite good in numerous different interviews. Ben Crenshaw and Geoff Ogilvy, players who also have a sense of golf history, also stood out. I also had a stats guru named Dave Fulp, who did an excellent job breaking down some of the numbers and providing some insight in ways that many may not have considered previously.
Quad: Nicklaus recently started an LLC called 20 Majors. What’d you make of that, and did you factor in their amateur wins in comparing the two?
BH: Well, I think 20 sounds better than 18, and certainly there was a time when Jack was credited with 20. During the final round of the 1986 Masters, CBS’ Pat Summerall referred to him chasing his 20th major. Afterward, Golf Digest, Sports Illustrated, the New Yorker, the Los Angeles Times, and the San Francisco Chronicle referred to it as 20 majors. But the Associated Press called it 18, so that far back there was already some differentiation. Nicklaus has said many times that he doesn’t exactly know when he lost the two majors. Arnold Palmer said the same thing about his U.S. Amateur title being dropped from his total of eight down to seven. I do mention all of this as a way of showing how the majors evolved over the years, and that counting the major titles was a way of harkening back to Bobby Jones. But for the purposes of keeping track, it’s Jack 18, Tiger 15, Walter Hagen 11. (If you want to talk about Hagen’s five Western Open titles when it was considered “major”, that’s another discussion that is also addressed.)
Quad: As a former Evans Scholar, where’d you loop the most, and if there was one course you could play or caddie at for eternity, what would it be?
BH: When I was a caddie, it was almost exclusively at one club that was less than two miles from where I grew up. Inverness Golf Club in Paltaine, Ill. To this day, I can probably remember some of the yardages from various landmarks on the course, one of the ways we were taught to keep track of those things before yardage books and certainly rangefinders became a thing. Not sure I want to caddie anywhere now! I could probably play North Berwick’s West Links every day if asked to pick just one. Not sure you can go wrong there.

Eight of the 26 U.S. Women’s Open qualifiers are in the books.
The results page.The Heroes Classic will be held for the first time on Tuesday, July 14th, as part of The 154th Open festivities at Royal Birkdale. The field will include Jordan Spieth and Pádraig Harrington, both former winners at Royal Birkdale, reigning AIG Women’s Open champion Miyu Yamashita, G4D Champion Brendan Lawlor, Tommy Fleetwood and Justin Rose, as well as “high-profile figures from sport and entertainment” including R&A ambassadors Bryan Habana and Kathryn Newton. The event will be contested in teams of three players over the first, second and ninth holes using a Texas scramble format
